articles.title: Ignite Fire Festival Returns to Rochdale from 20 to 22 November 2026
articles.excerpt: The Ignite Fire Festival will take place in Rochdale from 20 to 22 November 2026, featuring new displays and attractions for families to enjoy.
articles.content_html:
The Ignite Fire Festival will return to Rochdale for three evenings of entertainment from Friday, 20 November to Sunday, 22 November 2026. Organisers promise that this year's event will be bigger and better, featuring new dazzling trails and attractions.

The festival will transform the square and gardens around Rochdale Town Hall, including new pathways and parkland on Broadfield Slopes. Last year, the festival attracted over 10,000 attendees, and this year, new displays will be available for visitors to walk through each evening.

Highlights will include fiery displays, blazing sculptures, and an illuminated installation created by the award-winning outdoor arts specialists Walk the Plank. The Christmas lights switch-on will also take place on the final evening of the festival, adding to the festive atmosphere.

Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Borough Council, expressed enthusiasm for the event, stating that it will offer magical and immersive trails of fire, lights, and sound. Further details about the festival will be announced in October.

articles.title: Rochdale Town Hall Features in New BBC Legal Drama The Split Up
articles.excerpt: The BBC's new legal drama, The Split Up, filmed at Rochdale Town Hall, showcases the historic council chamber as a courtroom setting, featuring notable actors including Lenny Henry.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Town Hall has been transformed into a filming location for the new BBC legal drama, The Split Up, which premieres this Sunday. The series, created by Ursula Rani Sarma and based on Abi Morgan's acclaimed show The Split, features a storyline centred around a Manchester-based family law firm, Kishan Law, known for handling high-net-worth divorce cases.

The historic council chamber of Rochdale Town Hall, which once served as a magistrates' court, has been restored to highlight its original features, providing an authentic backdrop for the courtroom scenes. The series stars Sanjeev Bhaskar as Dhruv, the patriarch and head of the law firm, alongside Ritu Arya, who plays his ambitious daughter, Aria, poised to take over the family business following the death of her mother.

Rochdale Council has encouraged residents to tune in and spot the town hall in the new series, which aims to reflect the complexities of family law and the personal struggles of its characters. The filming in Rochdale adds to the town's growing reputation as a location for television and film productions.

As The Split Up airs, viewers can expect to see the town hall prominently featured, showcasing its architectural beauty and historical significance. This production not only highlights local talent but also promotes Rochdale as a vibrant filming destination, potentially attracting future projects to the area.

articles.title: Why does Rochdale say 'cruckle'?
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the local verb 'cruckle' — what it means, where it comes from, and why Rochdale people still claim it as their own.
articles.summary: A short guide to the local verb 'cruckle' — what it means, where it comes from, and why Rochdale people still claim it as their own.
articles.body:
If you grew up in parts of Rochdale you will probably recognise the line: “I cruckled my ankle.” Locally, to “cruckle” is used to mean rolling or twisting the ankle — that awkward stumble you can often walk off but which still makes you wince.

That everyday meaning is reflected in recent research into how people label and describe accents and local speech across Greater Manchester. A 2024 perceptual‑dialectology study (draw‑a‑map / keywords method) recorded people naming “cruckle” among the words they associate with Rochdale speech, alongside other locally salient terms such as guinnel (ginnel) and “broad”. The study’s maps and sample (hundreds of contributors from the ten GM boroughs) show that, whether by habit or pride, many respondents link the word specifically to Rochdale.

But “cruckle” is not a brand‑new invention. Historical dialect lexicons record older forms such as crookle (and variants) with meanings in the same semantic field — to bend, make crooked, stoop, hobble — senses that naturally extend to tripping, stumbling or going over on a foot. Late‑19th and early‑20th‑century dialect material and comparative work on Germanic vocabularies point to a family of related words (crook‑, kruk‑ types) across northern English and Scots dialects and into Scandinavian dialects; the picture is of an old verb pattern that local communities have kept alive in different forms.

The Dictionary of the Scots Language and related dialect sources list cognate forms (cruggle, cruckle, krukel, etc.) meaning to crouch, bend or huddle; the entries show how frequentative or imitative verb endings (‑le) and the crook/krug root produce senses of bending, stooping and halting movement. In short: linguists see cruckle as a predictable local survival of a wider, older dialect verb group rather than a completely isolated coinage.

Is cruckle unique to Rochdale? It depends how you look at it. On the one hand, folk‑linguistic evidence — what people say about accents and vocabulary — strongly ties the word to Rochdale: residents and others in the region often point to it as a local marker. On the other hand, dialect records show related forms elsewhere in northern England and in Scots dialects, so the root is regional rather than absolutely exclusive. What makes the word feel particularly “Rochdale” is the combination of continued local use, local recognition, and the way people use it as an emblem of home speech.

Why do dialect researchers care? Small words like cruckle are useful because they reveal two things at once: living speech practice (who still uses the word and where) and folk awareness (which terms people think define their place). Modern perceptual studies use crowd‑sourced mapping and keyword analysis to show where labels cluster and how they carry social meaning — for Rochdale, cruckle is one of those small but telling signals of local identity.

If you’re after a short take‑away: the word’s meaning — to roll or twist your ankle — matches local usage in Rochdale today; its form is part of a long‑standing northern dialect family (crookle/cruckle/kruggle); and research shows it is especially strongly associated with Rochdale in people’s perceptions, even while related forms appear elsewhere in historical records. If you don’t know the word, try using it next time you take a tumble in a ginnel — you’ll probably get a nod of recognition from someone from round here.

Note on sources: this piece draws on recent perceptual dialect research into Greater Manchester (Dann et al., Journal of Linguistic Geography, 2024), historical dialect lexicography and Scots dialect entries that document related forms, and reporting of the British Library’s dialect collecting work that records cruckle/crookle among regionally attested words.

articles.title: Ofsted Reports Published for Tiddlywinks Day Nursery and Willow View School
articles.excerpt: Ofsted has released new inspection reports for Tiddlywinks Day Nursery and Willow View School in Rochdale, both dated 17 September 2026, detailing their findings and ratings.
articles.content_html:
Ofsted has published inspection reports for Tiddlywinks Day Nursery and Willow View School, both located in Rochdale, on 17 September 2026. These reports provide insights into the quality of education and care provided at these institutions, along with any ratings awarded based on the inspections.

Tiddlywinks Day Nursery, which is registered on the Early Years Register, is subject to inspections at least once every four years, with additional inspections conducted if concerns arise. Newly registered settings are inspected within 18 months of registration. The latest report outlines the nursery's compliance with educational standards and its overall performance, although specific ratings and findings from the report have not been detailed in the summary.

Willow View School, classified as a non-association independent school, undergoes inspections every three years. The recent report reflects the school's adherence to educational guidelines and its effectiveness in delivering quality education. Ofsted also conducts additional inspections when commissioned by the Secretary of State for Education, ensuring that the school meets the required standards.

Both reports are accessible through the Ofsted website, where parents and guardians can subscribe for alerts regarding future inspections. These findings are significant for families in the Rochdale area, as they provide essential information about the quality of early years and educational services available to their children.

articles.title: Middleton Regeneration Plans Confirmed by Local Authorities
articles.excerpt: Middleton's regeneration plans are advancing with the announcement of new tenants for the Old Grammar School and the acquisition of Warwick Mill, as part of the Mayoral Development Corporation's initiatives.
articles.content_html:
Middleton's regeneration efforts have received a significant boost with a series of announcements aimed at revitalising the town. The Mayoral Development Corporation (MDC) is spearheading these initiatives, which include the recent acquisition of the historic Middleton Old Grammar School by Rochdale Council. The council is expected to announce a new tenant for the building before the end of the year, following a feasibility study to assess its potential for community use.

The Old Grammar School, located on Boarshaw Road, has a rich history dating back to its founding in 1582, originally established to provide free education to local children. In recent years, it served as a wedding and events venue until the council seized the opportunity to purchase the heritage asset when it became available for sale. Plans for its future include necessary repairs and refurbishments to reopen it for community activities.

The announcements were made during an event at Middleton Arena, which aimed to update residents and local businesses on the outcomes of an engagement exercise titled 'Our Town, Our Future.' The event was chaired by the proposed leaders of the MDC, Steve Coogan and Rose Marley, and attended by Mayor of Greater Manchester, Bev Craig, along with Rochdale Council leader, Cllr Neil Emmott. Over 500 residents and business leaders participated, highlighting the community's interest in the regeneration plans.

In addition to the Old Grammar School, the council is also in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill and the adjacent London House office block. The aim is to restore Warwick Mill for potential residential use while demolishing London House, which dates back to the 1960s. These developments are part of a broader strategy to enhance the town's infrastructure and community facilities, signalling a commitment to Middleton's ongoing regeneration.

articles.title: Heywood Police Stop Over 60 Vehicles in Anti-Social Driving Operation
articles.excerpt: Officers from the Heywood Neighbourhood Policing Team conducted a traffic enforcement operation on 16 September 2026, targeting anti-social driving and ensuring compliance with road safety regulations.
articles.content_html:
Officers from the Heywood Neighbourhood Policing Team carried out a traffic enforcement operation on 16 September 2026, as part of Operation Paragon, aimed at tackling anti-social driving in Heywood. This initiative involved collaboration with Rochdale Council licensing officers and the DVLA, responding to rising concerns about driving standards in the area.

During the operation, a static site was established for vehicle stops, resulting in over 60 vehicles being checked for various offences. These included violations categorised under the Fatal Five: speeding, drink and drug-driving, not wearing a seatbelt, using a mobile phone while driving, and careless driving.

PCSO Stewart, who planned the operation, stated that poor driving standards and a lack of responsibility among drivers contribute to injuries and unnecessary accidents. The operation aimed to ensure that taxis and other vehicles complied with licensing legislation and roadworthiness standards, enhancing road safety in the community.

The enforcement operation is part of ongoing efforts by local authorities and police to improve driving behaviour and reduce incidents of anti-social driving in Heywood. Further initiatives may follow as authorities continue to monitor and address these issues.

articles.title: Scout Moor II Wind Farm Plans Reduced Following Community Feedback
articles.excerpt: Developers have scaled back the Scout Moor II wind farm project, reducing the number of proposed turbines from 17 to 12 after consulting with local residents and organisations.
articles.content_html:
Developers have revised plans for the Scout Moor II wind farm, located on moorland between Rochdale and Rossendale, reducing the number of proposed turbines from 17 to 12. This decision follows feedback from local residents and organisations, aiming to address concerns raised during the initial consultation process.

The new wind farm will be situated adjacent to the existing Scout Moor wind farm, with each turbine potentially reaching heights of up to 590 feet (180 metres), making them taller than Blackpool Tower. The revised plans have been submitted to both Rochdale and Rossendale councils for further review and consultation before any approval is granted.

Campaign group Friends of the Moorland has expressed skepticism regarding the revisions, stating that it is unlikely all their concerns will be fully addressed. Steve Davison from the group indicated that a detailed review of the new plans is necessary to form a comprehensive opinion on the changes.

The initial proposals had attracted hundreds of objections, with opponents highlighting potential impacts on peatland, wildlife, and the surrounding landscape. The next steps will involve a further round of consultations, allowing the community to voice their opinions on the updated plans.
